new.title: Climb the Monument to the Battle of the Nations
new.desc: The 91-metre Völkerschlachtdenkmal was inaugurated in 1913 to mark the centenary of the 1813 Battle of Leipzig against Napoleon. Inside are a crypt with huge stone knights and a Hall of Fame; a viewing platform looks over the whole city.
new.tip: Tram 15 to Völkerschlachtdenkmal; the climb is about 500 steps. The reflecting pool in front is best photographed in the morning.

new.title: Visit Bach's grave in the Thomaskirche
new.desc: The Gothic Thomaskirche is the home church of the Thomanerchor and the place where Johann Sebastian Bach worked as Thomaskantor from 1723 until 1750. His tomb lies in the chancel, and the church has windows and a Bach statue outside.
new.tip: Entry to the church is free; the choir sings on Fridays at 18:00 and Saturdays at 15:00 outside holidays. Combine it with the Bach-Museum across the square.

new.title: See the palm-column nave of the Nikolaikirche
new.desc: Leipzig's oldest and largest city-centre church has a classical interior with palm-shaped pillars. Monday peace prayers held here since 1982 grew into the 1989 demonstrations that helped end the GDR.
new.tip: Free entry; peace prayers are on Mondays at 17:00. The Nikolaisäule column on the forecourt marks the story.

new.title: Admire the Renaissance Old Town Hall on the Markt
new.desc: Built in 1556 by mayor Hieronymus Lotter, the Altes Rathaus is one of Germany's finest Renaissance town halls. It houses the Stadtgeschichtliches Museum with Leipzig's city history.
new.tip: The museum is free for under-18s; the market square outside has stalls on Tuesdays, Fridays and Saturdays.

new.title: Climb the tower of the Neues Rathaus
new.desc: The New Town Hall opened in 1905 on the grounds of the old Pleißenburg and has the tallest town-hall tower in Germany at 114.7 metres. A viewing platform in the tower looks over the city centre.
new.tip: The tower is open on most days with small summer-only gaps; the entrance is on the Burgplatz side. Bring cash for the small fee.

new.title: Stroll through the Mädler Passage
new.desc: The Mädler-Passage opened in 1914 as one of the most beautiful covered shopping arcades in Europe, with Art Nouveau-influenced details. At its entrance stand the Faust and Mephisto bronze figures by Mathieu Molitor, and Auerbachs Keller lies beneath.
new.tip: Rub the toe of the Faust figure outside for luck. The arcade is free to walk through.

new.title: Step into Asisi's 360-degree world in the Panometer
new.desc: The former gasometer in Connewitz holds huge circular panoramas by artist Yadegar Asisi, with a visitor platform and an accompanying exhibition. The rotating subjects are shown in a 106-metre-circumference panorama.
new.tip: Check which panorama is currently shown; plan about an hour. It is close to tram stops in Connewitz.

new.title: See Beckmann and Cranach at the Museum der bildenden Künste
new.desc: The glass-cube MdbK on Katharinenstraße holds one of Germany's major municipal art collections, with Max Beckmann, Lucas Cranach, Caspar David Friedrich and the Leipzig School.
new.tip: Open Wednesday 12-20 and Thursday to Sunday 10-18; under-19s enter free.
new.q: Museum der bildenden Künste Leipzig, Katharinenstraße 10, Leipzig

new.title: Browse the GRASSI Museum of Applied Arts
new.desc: The Grassimuseum, built 1925-1929 in Art Deco style, houses the Museum of Applied Arts alongside the Museum of Musical Instruments and the Museum of Ethnography. The applied arts collection spans antiquity to modern design.
new.tip: Choose one of the three museums or buy a combination ticket. Closed on Mondays.
new.q: GRASSI Museum für Angewandte Kunst, Johannisplatz 5-11, Leipzig

new.title: Learn Bach's story in the Bach-Museum
new.desc: The Bach-Museum is in the Bose-Haus opposite the Thomaskirche, next to the house where the Bach family lived. The exhibition shows original manuscripts and interactive stations on Bach's Leipzig years.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday 10-18, free on the first Tuesday of the month. Audio guide is included.

new.title: Enter the Stasi Museum in the Runde Ecke
new.desc: The former district headquarters of the GDR's Ministry for State Security shows the history, structure and methods of the Stasi. Protesters occupied the building on 4 December 1989 to stop files being destroyed.
new.tip: Entry is free, audio guides are available, and the exhibition is mostly in German with English leaflets.
new.q: Museum in der Runden Ecke, Dittrichring 24, Leipzig

new.title: Look over Leipzig from the Panorama Tower
new.desc: At 142 metres the former university tower on Augustusplatz is the tallest building in Leipzig. A viewing platform on the 29th floor has a view of the city, the Neuseenland lakes and the Völkerschlachtdenkmal.
new.tip: The platform entrance costs only a few euros; go before sunset on a clear day.

new.title: Marvel at the halls of Leipzig Hauptbahnhof
new.desc: Opened in 1915, Leipzig Hauptbahnhof is one of Europe's largest terminus stations by floor area, with a monumental stone façade and a three-level shopping promenade built into the old halls.
new.tip: Walk the Promenaden shopping levels and look up at the great hall from the platforms.

new.title: See the golden-domed Russian Memorial Church
new.desc: The Russian Memorial Church was consecrated in 1913 to honour Russian soldiers killed at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813. It is a Novgorod-style church with a green-and-gold tower, and is still in use by the Russian Orthodox community.
new.tip: Open for visits at set hours; check times beforehand. Walk on to the Völkerschlachtdenkmal.

new.title: Wander the Baumwollspinnerei art quarter in Plagwitz
new.desc: Once the largest cotton mill on the European continent, founded in 1884, the Spinnerei now holds around a hundred studios and galleries, linked to the New Leipzig School. Visitors can walk the factory courtyards and brick halls.
new.tip: Galleries are generally open Tuesday to Saturday; the Rundgang open-studio weekends occur in spring and autumn.

new.title: Walk through the Botanischer Garten der Universität
new.desc: Founded in 1542, the University of Leipzig's botanical garden is one of the oldest in Germany. Greenhouses, a fragrance garden and systematic beds sit near the Grassi quarter.
new.tip: Outdoor grounds are free to enter in the open season; greenhouses are open on set days. Check winter opening hours.
new.q: Botanischer Garten der Universität Leipzig, Linnéstraße 1, Leipzig

new.title: Drink coffee in Germany's oldest coffee house
new.desc: Zum Arabischen Coffe Baum has served coffee since 1711 and was a haunt of Robert Schumann and other musicians. It reopened in April 2025 after six years of renovation with a Wiener Café and Café Français on separate floors.
new.tip: Try a Leipziger Lerche with a coffee; the museum upstairs is free and open daily 11-19.
new.q: Zum Arabischen Coffe Baum, Kleine Fleischergasse 4, Leipzig

new.title: Taste Leipziger Lerche at Café Kandler
new.desc: Café Kandler sits next to the Thomaskirche and bakes cakes by traditional recipes by hand. It is known for the Leipziger Lerche, the shortcrust tart with almonds and a cherry, and for the Bachtaler.
new.tip: Order a Lerche with a Bach-Kaffee; it is busy after the Thomaner motet.

new.title: Order an Elefantenkaffee at Kaffeehaus Riquet
new.desc: The Riquet house of 1908-09 combines Art Nouveau with Chinese-inspired architecture and elephant heads at the entrance. The café is one of the few traditional coffee houses left in the city centre.
new.tip: Try the Elefantenkaffee at a window table; reviews mention mixed service on busy days.

new.title: Drink Gose at the Gosenschenke Ohne Bedenken
new.desc: This Gohlis tavern is the revival of the old Gosenschenke tradition, reopened in 1986 by Lothar Goldhahn. It brews the sour, salty top-fermented Leipziger Gose and has a beer garden in the season.
new.tip: Open Wednesday to Sunday; confirm hours as the beer garden is seasonal. Order a Gose with a Leipziger Allerlei or Bratwurst.

new.title: Taste Leipziger Gose at the Bayerischer Bahnhof
new.desc: Built 1841-44 as the terminus of the Leipzig-Hof line, the Bayerischer Bahnhof held the world's oldest railway terminus until 2011. Its Gasthaus & Gosebrauerei brews the Leipziger Gose on site in a microbrewery.
new.tip: Try the Gose with a coriander shot; a Saxon menu is served.
new.q: Gasthaus & Gosebrauerei Bayerischer Bahnhof, Bayrischer Platz 1, Leipzig

new.title: Dine in Goethe's Faust cellar, Auerbachs Keller
new.desc: Auerbachs Keller beneath the Mädler Passage has been a wine tavern since the 16th century and is the setting of a scene in Goethe's Faust. The historic vaults offer Saxon dishes in the Großer Keller and a gourmet restaurant.
new.tip: Reserve ahead for dinner; try Saxon dishes such as Leipziger Allerlei.

new.title: Eat Saxon fare at the Thüringer Hof
new.desc: The Thüringer Hof is a historic inn serving regional dishes since 1454, a place where Goethe and Schumann are said to have eaten. It has several connected vaulted rooms.
new.tip: Order a regional dish such as Leipziger Allerlei or beef roulade; the courtyard fills up in summer.

new.title: Try Leipziger Allerlei at Barthels Hof
new.desc: Barthels Hof is a historic trade-fair courtyard near the Markt, now a restaurant serving Leipzig classics. Leipziger Allerlei is a vegetable dish with crayfish, served alongside beef roulade, the Leipziger Lerche and Gose beer.
new.tip: Order the Allerlei with a Gose; the courtyard is pleasant in summer.

new.title: Sip a cocktail in the Mephisto Bar
new.desc: The Mephisto Bar in the Mädler Passage serves coffee specialities by day and cocktails with live music in the evenings. The setting echoes the Faust theme of the arcade.
new.tip: Come for a coffee by day or music at night; check the event calendar.
new.q: Mephisto Bar, Mädler-Passage, Grimmaische Straße 2-4, Leipzig

new.title: Hear the Thomanerchor sing a Motette
new.desc: The Thomanerchor, founded in 1212, performs a Motette on Fridays at 18:00 and Saturdays at 15:00 in the Thomaskirche. Special Gewandhaus and Thomanerchor concerts feature Bach works.
new.tip: Tickets are cheap for regular motets; not held during holidays or tours.

new.title: Catch a performance at the Oper Leipzig
new.desc: The Opernhaus on Augustusplatz, opened in 1960, is one of Germany's oldest opera companies, with a repertoire of opera and ballet.
new.tip: Standing and last-minute tickets are cheaper; check the season schedule.

new.title: Attend a Gewandhausorchester concert
new.desc: The Gewandhaus is home to the Gewandhausorchester, one of the world's oldest civic orchestras, founded in 1743. The Großer Saal, opened 1981, is known for its acoustics.
new.tip: Book via the box office; Beethoven Festival Leipzig takes place in 2027.

new.title: Paddle the Karl-Heine-Kanal through Plagwitz
new.desc: The Karl-Heine-Kanal, begun in 1856 by Karl Heine, runs through Plagwitz and Lindenau past old industrial buildings to the Lindenauer Hafen, which was connected to the Weiße Elster in 2015.
new.tip: Rent canoes or SUP boards from local providers; spring to autumn is best.

new.title: Swim at the Cospudener See north beach
new.desc: The Cospudener See, a flooded former lignite pit, has Saxony's longest sand beach. Swimming, sailing and stand-up paddling are popular here.
new.tip: Reach it by tram 11 and a short walk; swimming is a summer activity.

new.title: Walk and picnic in Clara-Zetkin-Park
new.desc: The Clara-Zetkin-Park was formed in 1955 from several older parks. It is Leipzig's central green space, with meadows, the Pleiße and jogging paths running into the Auwald.
new.tip: Free all year; rent a rowing boat on the canals in summer.

new.title: Walk the Rosental to the zoo's window
new.desc: The Rosental is a park-like area of about 118 hectares in the northern Auwald, bordered by the Elstermühlgraben, the Parthe and the zoo.
new.tip: Look for the viewing window onto the zoo's savanna area; free to enter.

new.title: Visit Zoo Leipzig and its Gondwanaland
new.desc: Founded in 1878 by Ernst Pinkert, Zoo Leipzig covers about 23 hectares and holds over 800 species. It is known for the Pongoland great ape enclosure and the tropical Gondwanaland hall.
new.tip: Allow half a day; buy tickets online to avoid queues.

new.title: Cycle through the Leipziger Auwald
new.desc: The Leipziger Auwald is one of Europe's largest floodplain forests in a city, running through the city from north to south along the Weiße Elster and Pleiße.
new.tip: Hire a bike and take the trail from Connewitz to the Schleußig; mosquitoes in summer.

new.title: Stroll Karli from Südvorstadt to Connewitz
new.desc: Karl-Liebknecht-Straße, locally Karli, runs from the centre through Südvorstadt to Connewitz. It is lined with cafes, bars, shops and street art, and is a nightlife area.
new.tip: Walk the stretch between Südplatz and Connewitz Kreuz in the evening.

new.title: Walk through the Palmengarten in Lindenau
new.desc: The Palmengarten is a park of 22.5 hectares in Leipzig-Lindenau, with a landscape garden and ponds.
new.tip: Free all year, good with a walk to the Karl-Heine-Kanal.
